item.title: Nation to revamp train numbering system
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
Nation to revamp train numbering system China will overhaul its train numbering system to accommodate the expansion of its railway network, changing the meaning of several familiar letter prefixes while keeping routes and schedules unchanged under the current timetable. The changes, to be introduced in late November and late December, will increase the number of available train numbers for bullet train services by nearly 40 percent, China State Railway Group, the national railway operator, said on Friday. For travelers, including international visitors, the key change is that letters long associated with one type of train will identify another. T and K, previously used for regular speed express and fast trains, will identify high-speed services with top operating speeds of 300 kilometers per hour and 200 to 250 km/h, respectively. G will identify Fuxing trains with a maximum operating speed of 350 km/h. The X prefix will be reserved for Fuxing trains operating above 350 km/h. However, no X series passenger services will begin operating in this round of changes, said Xu Yan, deputy director of the operator's passenger transport center. The overhaul follows substantial growth in railway services. Between 2014 and 2025, China's railway network expanded from 112,000 kilometers to 165,000 km, while the average number of passenger trains operating daily rose from 4,894 to 11,796. "During peak travel periods such as the May Day and National Day holidays, G series services use more than 90 percent of the available train numbers for that prefix," said Fan Mingxiang, deputy director of the operator's transport department. Wei Yuguang, a professor at Beijing Jiaotong University, said train numbers serve purposes far beyond helping passengers find their trains. "They are a common language for coordination across regions and departments," he said, explaining that each train's unique number is a basic unit for organizing transport, dispatching, passenger services and accounting. Even the length of a number matters. "Using three digits or four may mean just one extra word each time for a dispatcher, but repeated throughout the day, it adds considerably to the workload," Wei said. Pronunciation also needs to be considered. "If two train numbers sound very similar, that can cause problems in dispatching," he said. Wei said the new system builds on existing rules while making room for more trains and new services. It must accommodate both passenger and freight trains, including those operating across borders. Cross-border passenger services will also have their train numbers adjusted on domestic sections of their routes under the revised rules, the operator said. Regular speed passenger trains, tourist trains and some freight services will have their numbers changed in late November, followed by high-speed and other services in late December. The new train numbers will appear on 12306, China's official railway booking platform, when tickets go on sale, up to 15 days before departure. Onboard services, including quiet carriages and online meal ordering, will remain unchanged. For international visitors who rely on travel guides to plan their trips, older explanations of train prefixes may no longer apply after the changes. The operator urged passengers to check train numbers, departure and arrival stations, and schedules carefully.

item.title: Boost Sino-African educational ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
Boost Sino-African educational ties The future of China-Africa relations hinges significantly on the collaborative efforts of our universities. Universities are not merely institutions that hand out degrees; they are epicenters of knowledge, developers of human capital, incubators of innovation and custodians of cultural heritage. Higher education is being reshaped by artificial intelligence, automation, biotechnology, climate change, renewable energy and the fourth industrial revolution, all of which are redefining the skills that societies need. For Africa, these shifts present both opportunities and challenges. While the continent has the world's youngest population and enormous human potential, its universities still struggle due to limited access, quality issues, financial constraints, inadequate infrastructure and a widening gap between education and the labor market. The challenge is no longer about producing more graduates, but about cultivating graduates who can generate knowledge, create employment and devise solutions. China's remarkable transformation offers educational lessons. Decades of investment in education, science and technology have made Chinese universities global centers of innovation. Africa's task is not to duplicate that experience but to learn from it, adapt it and forge partnerships that leverage the unique strengths of both regions. Historically, university cooperation has focused on exchanges, scholarships, conferences and memoranda of understanding. While these remain useful, the focus should now move from exchange to transformation, from mobility to joint knowledge creation, from joint research outputs to patents and commercialization, and from agreements on paper to practical partnerships. We must explore what Chinese and African universities can achieve together that neither could do alone. We need partnerships that foster joint research programs, innovation hubs, laboratories, graduate schools and centers of excellence. This includes more joint PhDs and co-supervision, and deeper collaboration in AI, digital education, renewable energy, climate change, agriculture, health, manufacturing, engineering, entrepreneurship and the creative industries. The focus should be on African development priorities while addressing global challenges. Tanzania illustrates these possibilities. Our relationship with China dates back to the early 1960s, marked by infrastructure projects such as the Tanzania-Zambia Railway and now spanning scholarships, research collaboration and institutional partnerships. At the University of Dar es Salaam, cooperation through the Confucius Institute has promoted academic exchange, people-to-people and cultural understanding and capacity building. The lesson is clear: sustainable cooperation grows from mutual respect, shared interests and clearly defined practical outcomes. Future partnerships must evolve beyond traditional mobility and capacity-building toward co-creation and innovation — from student exchange to joint talent development, from academic visits to joint research, from technology transfer to joint innovation, from memoranda of understanding to measurable institutional outcomes, and from individual projects to strategic, long-term partnerships. Talent development is a critical area where China and Africa must intensify cooperation. Africa needs young people equipped to work with emerging technologies, launch enterprises and solve complex problems; China brings experience in large-scale human-capital development, technological education and innovation ecosystems. Our universities should build joint talent platforms linking students, academics, industry and government, with reciprocal mobility, joint master's and doctoral programs and blended-learning arrangements. The aim is a new generation of professionals who understand both societies. Digital transformation is another major frontier. China has deep experience in digital infrastructure, educational technology and large-scale online learning; African universities will benefit if cooperation addresses our realities: connectivity, affordability, devices, skills and the urban-rural divide. We should create joint China-Africa digital education platforms for cross-continental teaching and resource sharing. AI should also be a major area of collaboration. However, as we embrace AI, we must address ethics, academic integrity, data governance, privacy, equity and the responsible use of technology. Universities on both sides should develop technological capacity and ethical frameworks together. Partnerships must be judged by the knowledge and solutions they produce. China and Africa should define joint research agendas where interests converge: climate change and environmental sustainability; renewable energy and the energy transition; food security and agricultural transformation; public health; digital transformation and AI; critical minerals and value addition; manufacturing and industrialization; urbanization and sustainable cities; education and skills development; entrepreneurship and employment creation. The principle is simple: we should research jointly, and translate that into joint publications, patents, innovations, enterprises and policy solutions. China-Africa cooperation cannot be a one-way model of transfer. Our universities should embrace knowledge co-creation, with African and Chinese scholars as equal partners in defining questions, designing methods and translating findings into practice. The goal should not be "What can China do for Africa?" or "What can Africa do for China?", but "What can China and Africa do together for both and for humanity?" The next generation of cooperation should move beyond a collection of agreements toward a more integrated model that builds deeper strategic partnerships, brings researchers, students, industry and policymakers together through joint centers of excellence, and develops talent through scholarships, joint degrees, doctoral training, co-supervision and reciprocal mobility. The goal is to turn these networks and skills into joint innovation, translating research into products, enterprises, technologies and services. Ultimately, cooperation should be judged by what it produces — graduates, innovations, enterprises and practical solutions — rather than by the number of agreements signed or delegations exchanged. The frontiers of educational development are no longer bounded by individual institutions or national borders. They are defined by our capacity to connect knowledge, people and technology across them. Higher education must become a more strategic pillar of the China-Africa relationship. For Tanzania, we remain committed to strengthening cooperation with China not as a recipient of aid, but as a partner with whom we can co-create knowledge, develop talent and advance innovation. China-Africa university cooperation should move from partners in exchange to partners in development, from recipients of knowledge to co-creators of knowledge, and from isolated institutions into interconnected engines of transformation. As the Father of the Nation of Tanzania, Julius Nyerere, emphasized in his address, "the role of universities", more than six decades ago, universities in developing countries must not simply receive knowledge; they must contribute to it as well. His vision underscores the importance of mutual contribution and knowledge creation, a principle that remains central to China-Africa university cooperation today. Our greatest achievement will not be stronger universities but a generation of young Africans and Chinese equipped to build a more prosperous, innovative and shared future. The author is the vice-chancellor of the University of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The article is adapted from his keynote speech at the China-Africa University Presidents Forum on Frontiers of Education Development. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily. item.title: Red spirit spurs green growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March (1934-36), bringing renewed attention to the spirit of this defining chapter in Chinese history. Beyond its place in the national memory as a declaration, a publicity force and "sower of seeds", the Long March continues to shape contemporary efforts to link revolutionary heritage with economic and social development. Red tourism has emerged as a driver of rural vitalization and local economic growth. In Jiangxi, Guizhou and Sichuan provinces, the development of revolutionary sites and themed attractions has drawn visitors, boosted local services and encouraged improvements in infrastructure. The resulting tourism revenue has also created opportunities to raise residents' incomes. Beyond its economic impact, red tourism offers a way to pass historical memory and revolutionary traditions on to new generations. Local governments are also drawing on revolutionary history through educational programs and cultural activities. Schools, communities and enterprises organize events that introduce people to the country's revolutionary past and seek to strengthen patriotism and cultural confidence. Preserving the legacy of the Long March is therefore not only about remembering history. By connecting revolutionary resources with local development and environmental goals, communities are exploring ways to carry its spirit into a new era.

item.title: Xi: Prioritize ecological conservation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Xi: Prioritize ecological conservation He stresses green development on Inner Mongolia inspection tour President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to coordinate high-quality development with high-level protection of the environment, and underlined the need to unswervingly follow the path of prioritizing ecological conservation and pursuing green development. Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks on Friday during an inspection tour in Ulaanqab, Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Noting that green development is an essential aspect of high-quality growth, he urged a holistic approach to the conservation of mountains, rivers, forests, farmlands, lakes, grasslands and deserts, and called for efforts to promote carbon reduction, pollution reduction, green expansion and growth in a coordinated manner. Xi visited the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve, where he heard reports on the autonomous region's efforts to strengthen local ecological conservation, particularly enhance environmental governance and restore the ecosystem of Huangqihai Lake, an inland lake that was once on the verge of drying up due to climatic and other factors. He underlined the need to protect the wetlands, with focus on enhancing the quality and stability of ecosystems while maintaining biodiversity. With abundant wind and solar resources, Ulaanqab has leveraged its advantages in terms of location, climate and green electricity to develop the green computing industry, achieving significant progress. In the Qahar High-tech Industrial Development Zone, Xi learned about the progress of the "East Data, West Computing" project, a megaproject that aims to coordinate the computing capabilities of the country's eastern regions with inland western regions, as well as the development of green computing in Inner Mongolia. He pointed out that implementing the "East Data, West Computing" project and building an integrated national computing network is an important decision made by the CPC Central Committee. Xi emphasized the need to strengthen scientific planning, resources support and security assurance to ensure that existing projects are operated in an efficient manner and that projects still under construction are completed as scheduled. Efforts should be made to extend the industrial chain and promote the deep integration of the digital economy with the real economy, continuously transforming the strength in computing into development advantages, he said. While interacting with project leaders, technicians and staff members of the development zone, Xi emphasized that the computing network is one of the "six networks" planned and constructed by the country, and it is in a stage of accelerated development with broad prospects. China is accelerating a sweeping infrastructure plan centered around "six networks" — water, power, computing, telecommunications, urban pipelines and logistics — in order to stabilize investment, create jobs and lay the groundwork for the next phase of the country's technological and industrial transformation. Highlighting the importance of "computing-electricity synergy" and "computing-water synergy", Xi encouraged them to ensure smooth construction and operation of computing center projects and play an active role in the development of green computing, thereby contributing more to the building of a digital China and promoting the development of new quality productive forces. In 2025, Inner Mongolia generated more than 270 billion kilowatt-hours of renewable power, ranking among the top regions nationwide. This clean energy provides a stable power supply for energy-intensive data centers. As of July this year, the autonomous region's total computing power reached 345,000 PFlops, a unit representing one quadrillion calculations per second. Notably, over 85 percent of the electricity used by regional data centers comes from green power. Inner Mongolia has developed a dual-hub strategy centered in Hohhot, the regional capital, and Ulaanqab. The two centers operate in synergy and complement each other, efficiently handling high-intensity artificial intelligence computing tasks for both industrial and public sectors. During his tour, Xi also inspected local distinctive agricultural and livestock products, and encouraged the region to strengthen links between production and sales to increase incomes for local farmers and herdsmen. He emphasized that China is vast, with significant differences in resource endowments across its various regions. All regions should build on their respective conditions, leverage their comparative advantages, and pursue high-quality development tailored to local circumstances, he said. Xi's last inspection trip to Inner Mongolia was in June 2023. During that tour, he had urged the autonomous region to consolidate its role as a vital ecological barrier in northern China — the country's important base for energy and strategic resources, its important production base for agricultural commodities and livestock, and a vital gateway for opening-up to countries and regions north of China.

item.title: Cook says China is key to iPhone Duo's success
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Cook says China is key to iPhone Duo's success Apple's first foldable smartphone is manufactured exclusively in China and Chinese app developers are crucial to iPhone Duo's success, Tim Cook, Apple's executive chairman, said in a recent exclusive interview with China Daily in Beijing. The remarks underline the great importance of China to United States tech companies such as Apple, as China is not just a huge market, but also an innovation center and a key manufacturing hub for their global operations, experts said. Cook said Chinese developers' enthusiasm for the foldable device and China's manufacturing capabilities are part of the recipe behind iPhone Duo's success. "We are working with a number of developers and optimizing some of the things at (our) Shanghai developer center. The apps are extremely important to us, and we're helping hand in hand," he said, adding that Chinese developers play a critical role in that process and they're very innovative. "China's market for foldables is second to none," Cook added. As Apple's first foldable model, iPhone Duo is far more difficult to manufacture than previous products. According to Apple, the process requires strong manufacturing precision and design capabilities, and it manages that through close collaboration with suppliers. Bai Ming, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, said, "China's decades of experience in electronics manufacturing and its continued push to pursue advanced and smart manufacturing make it the only country capable of making complicated products such as iPhone Duo." Cook is on a multi-stop visit to China, touring cities including Guangzhou in Guangdong province, Beijing and Shanghai. On Friday, Cook said at a forum in Shanghai that China's artificial intelligence application landscape is showing unprecedented dynamism, and AI is already having a profound impact on Apple's supply chain. During the trip, the senior executive also said that Apple Intelligence — which incorporates Chinese tech company Alibaba's Qwen large language model — has received approval in China and a test version is set to launch later this month. On Thursday, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao met Cook in Beijing, where they exchanged views on issues including China-US economic and trade relations. Notably, Cook said that Apple will further expand its business in China. Cook's visit came amid a wave of top US business executives' recent visits to China. Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater Associates, also visited Beijing this week. Sean Stein, president of the US-China Business Council, said the planet's most innovative companies are concentrated in the US and China, which lays a solid foundation for wider cooperation. "Such collaboration stretches well beyond one, two or even three industries — a reflection of a deliberate effort by firms on both sides to learn from each other and forge partnerships across the globe," Stein said. According to a report released by the American Chamber of Commerce in South China earlier this year, 75 percent of enterprises it surveyed plan to reinvest in China in 2026, and over the next three to five years, its member companies are expected to reinvest $13.79 billion in profits generated in China. Gong Yu, founder and CEO of Chinese video-streaming company iQiyi — which Cook visited during his trip — said the ties between the two companies can be dated back to 2010. "Innovation in hardware, including the application of AI technology, has given us a particularly good synergy. This kind of mechanism allows us to achieve one plus one bigger than two, enabling this synergy to unleash even greater value," Gong said.
